concept.body: Central angle vs interior angle: the CENTRAL angle sits at the circle's MIDDLE (360 ÷ n), while the INTERIOR angle sits at a VERTEX of the polygon (180(n−2)/n). For a hexagon they're 60° and 120° — never mix them up.

explanationVariants: The central angle of a regular hexagon is 360 ÷ 6 = 60°.
"At the center" means divide the full turn: 360 ÷ 6.

widget.prompt: What is the CENTRAL angle (at the circle's center) for a regular hexagon, in degrees?

commonErrors.feedback: 120° is the INTERIOR angle at a vertex. The CENTRAL angle divides the full turn: 360 ÷ 6 = 60°.
30° would be 360 ÷ 12 — too many slices. A hexagon has 6 vertices: 360 ÷ 6 = 60°.

steps.body: The compass hides a gift: **the radius of a circle steps around it exactly six times**. Keep the compass set to the circle's radius, walk it point-to-point around the circle, and the six marks are the vertices of a perfect regular hexagon. No measuring — the radius IS the side.
Why the hexagon falls out of the circle.

predict.prompt: You will step the compass around a circle of radius 6. What compass opening lands you exactly back at the start after six steps?

options.label: 3 — half the radius, since six steps is a lot
About 6.3 — a sixth of the circumference

predict.reveal: The radius itself. A chord equal to the radius makes an equilateral triangle with the two radii to its ends, so it subtends exactly 60° — and six 60° steps is one full lap. Set the compass to 6 and walk it round.

widget.prompt: The circle has radius 6. Set the compass so that stepping it round the circle lands exactly back at the start after six steps.
widget.successFeedback: Compass = 6, the radius itself. A chord equal to the radius makes an equilateral triangle with the two radii to its ends, so it subtends exactly 60° — and six 60° steps is one full lap. The hexagon is not a construction you memorise; it is the only shape a compass set to its own circle's radius can make.
widget.lowFeedback: Your steps are too small, so more than six of them are needed to get round.
widget.highFeedback: Your steps are too big, so fewer than six get you round — and they overshoot the start.

cml.actionGoal: Change the compass radius and observe the exact equal-distance guarantees created by intersecting arcs.

explanationVariants: Each hexagon vertex spans a 60° central angle, and a chord across 60° in a radius-r circle has length exactly r. Six 60° arcs fill 360°, so the radius fits six times.
The triangle from the center to two adjacent vertices has two radius sides and a 60° apex — an equilateral triangle, so its third side (the chord) also equals r.

widget.prompt: Why does the radius step around a circle exactly six times?

options.label: Each step spans a 60° central angle, and a 60° chord equals the radius
options.feedback: Center-to-two-adjacent-vertices makes an equilateral triangle (two radii, 60° apex), so the chord equals r — and six 60° arcs complete 360°.

options.label: The compass naturally makes six equal parts
options.feedback: The compass just holds ONE length. Six steps is a consequence of the 60°-chord-equals-radius fact, not a property of the tool.

options.label: A circle has six sides
options.feedback: A circle has no sides at all. The six comes from equilateral triangles fitting around the center.

options.label: Because 360 ÷ 60 happens to be six, by coincidence
options.feedback: It's no coincidence — the 60° itself comes from the equilateral triangle formed by two radii and the chord.

steps.body: That center triangle is the key: two radii plus the chord, with a 60° angle between the radii. Two equal sides and a 60° angle between them force an **equilateral** triangle — so all three sides, chord included, equal the radius. Six such triangles tile the hexagon like pizza slices.

widget.prompt: A regular hexagon's six vertices divide the full 360° around the center equally. What is the central angle for each vertex, in degrees?

commonErrors.feedback: 120° is the hexagon's INTERIOR angle (at a vertex), not the CENTRAL angle. Divide the full turn by 6: 360 ÷ 6 = 60°.
6 is the number of vertices, not an angle. The central angle is the full turn split among them: 360 ÷ 6 = 60°.

explanationVariants: A regular hexagon's interior angle is 180(6−2)/6 = 720/6 = 120°.
Six triangles each contribute two 60° base angles at a vertex: 60 + 60 = 120° interior.

widget.prompt: What is the measure of each INTERIOR angle of a regular hexagon, in degrees?

commonErrors.feedback: 60° is the CENTRAL angle (at the middle). The interior angle at a vertex is larger: 180(6−2)/6 = 120°.
720° is the SUM of all six interior angles. Each one is 720 ÷ 6 = 120°.

hints: The six center-to-vertex triangles are all equilateral — what's each one's apex angle?
Each apex is 60°. Connecting every OTHER vertex skips one each time.
Skipping one vertex doubles the central angle to 120°, giving 3 vertices.
explanationVariants: Joining every other hexagon vertex uses 3 of the 6 marks, each spanning 120° (two 60° steps) — a regular triangle, the inscribed equilateral.
Alternate vertices sit 120° apart; three of them at 120° each fill 360° — an equilateral triangle.

widget.prompt: Starting from an inscribed hexagon, you connect every OTHER vertex. What shape appears?

options.label: an equilateral triangle
options.feedback: Three of the six marks, each 120° apart — a regular (equilateral) triangle inscribed in the same circle.

options.label: a smaller hexagon
options.feedback: Skipping vertices REDUCES the count from 6 to 3 — you get a triangle, not another hexagon.

options.label: a square
options.feedback: A square needs 4 vertices 90° apart. Every-other of 6 gives 3 vertices 120° apart — a triangle.

options.label: a regular pentagon
options.feedback: A pentagon needs 5 vertices; the hexagon's marks are spaced for multiples of 60°, which never give 72° pentagon spacing.

takeaways: The circle's radius steps around it exactly six times — the hexagon needs no measuring.
It works because each center triangle (two radii + 60°) is equilateral, so the chord equals r.
Central angle 60°, interior angle 120°; joining alternate vertices gives the inscribed equilateral triangle.
